items.prompt: The finance ministry plans next year's public services: it expects N$64 billion of revenue and intends N$72 billion of spending on schools, clinics and roads. Define the government budget.
items.canonical_answer: The government budget is the government's yearly plan of the revenue it expects to raise - most of it from taxation - set beside the spending it intends to carry out on public services. In this case the plan pairs expected revenue of N$64 billion with intended spending of N$72 billion; because the spending exceeds the revenue, the plan also implies a year of borrowing.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: a yearly plan of expected revenue set beside intended spending, not the cash the government happens to hold.
The meaning must pair both sides of the plan - revenue and spending; a definition that names the spending while leaving the revenue out earns little.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Namibia's budget statement arrives each year with revenue estimates on one side and departmental spending plans on the other. Identify the features a government budget includes.
items.canonical_answer: A government budget includes a statement of expected revenue - the tax and other receipts the government forecasts it will raise; a plan of intended spending, set out department by department for services such as schooling, health care and roads; and, where the two sides do not match, the borrowing that bridges the difference. Together these state the fiscal stance for the year ahead.
marking_guidance: Reward the features named - expected revenue, intended spending and any borrowing that bridges the gap - as parts of the yearly plan.
What it includes must be features of the plan itself; a list of things the government happens to spend on, with no plan element around them, earns little.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: Street lighting over Otavi's taxi rank cannot be confined to those who pay for it, so no private firm installs any. Define the reason for government spending this market shows.
items.canonical_answer: The reason is the under-provision of public goods: because the benefits of a public good cannot be confined to those who pay - non-payers cannot be excluded, and one user's use leaves as much for the next - private firms tend to provide too little of it, so the government steps in and funds it from the budget.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: under-provision of public goods, with the two features that explain why the market left alone tends to provide too little.
The meaning must state why the market fails to fund the lighting; a definition that treats public spending as good in itself earns little.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: The budget commits N$500 million to resurfacing the road from Outjo to the Etosha gate, with road crews in the district idle and lodges along the route paying some of the region's lowest wages. Analyse the consequences of this spending for the road crews, the lodges and the government's budget.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the initial change is N$500 million of public spending committed to the resurfacing, arriving in a district with idle crews - spare capacity among builders. Mechanism: because contractors hiring the crews pay wages that then circulate through the towns along the route, this causes household incomes to rise where people were idle, and the lodges' trade grows as the improved road lowers the cost and risk of the journey for visitors. Consequence: therefore the crews gain work and wages, the lodges gain trade and their workers gain hours, and the government's budget carries the N$500 million outlay now, to be financed from revenue or borrowing and, where borrowed, repaid from later budgets. For whom: work and wages for the road crews and their firms; trade for the lodges and their staff; the financing and any repayment for the taxpayer.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - N$500 million committed to resurfacing - must be named first, together with the idle crews.
Mechanism: because the spending reaches workers with spare capacity, this causes incomes and then trade to rise; the wage chain must be traced.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the crews, the lodges and their workers, the budget - needs its own traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the road crews, the lodge staff, the taxpayer.

items.prompt: The state clinic in Gobabis treats 4 000 patients a season free of charge, while a private pharmacy on the same street sells the same treatments to those who can pay. Explain, for this town, why the government rather than the pharmacy funds the clinic.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the figures show treatment given free to all 4 000 patients regardless of payment, which a private seller does not do - the clinic is a merit good, judged worth more to the town than households asked to pay would consume. The reasoning: because households that cannot pay would go untreated by a private seller, the market left alone tends to provide less treatment than the town needs, and the link to the government's role is that correction of under-consumption - provision from the budget also transfers care towards households that could not buy it. Conclusion: therefore the state funds the clinic from the budget so that treatment depends on need rather than payment, and the pharmacy's trade stays limited to what buyers choose to pay for.
marking_guidance: The context - the figures: 4 000 patients treated free against the pharmacy's paying customers - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because untreated households make the under-consumption real, the link is the merit-good case for public provision.
Conclusion: therefore the answer must close the loop on why the state pays and the private seller does not.

items.prompt: The ministry can either spend N$1.2 billion over three years on free textbooks and school meals for the poorest regions or use the same sum to cut taxes for small firms. Discuss whether the spending programme is the better use of the N$1.2 billion.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement, on balance: the spending programme is likely to serve the reasons for government spending better, though it depends on whether the school schemes reach the classrooms they target and on how firms would use a tax cut. Why it might: the textbooks and meals are merit goods that households on low incomes under-consume when left to pay themselves, so public provision reaches children whose families cannot buy them; the meals transfer spending power towards the poorest households, narrowing the income gap; and the money flows straight into schools rather than waiting on firms to choose to invest. Why it might not: small firms may take a tax cut and hire, and where there is spare capacity that raises output and jobs, serving the employment and growth aims directly; the schemes may leak into administration; and meals supplied from central depots may displace local food sellers' trade. The condition: what settles it is delivery - whether the school schemes reach the regions they target, and whether firms facing the tax cut would hire or merely hold the sum; judged on reach to the poorest, the programme is the stronger case, judged on speed to jobs, the cut may be.
marking_guidance: The judgement must be stated and be decisive: on balance the programme or the cut, with its reason.
Why it might: the case for - merit-good provision and redistribution reaching the poorest households - developed to its consequence.
Why it might not: the case against - firms hiring where there is spare capacity, delivery leaking, trade displaced - developed to its own consequence.
The condition it depends on: what settles it is delivery against the firms' hiring response; answers that name no decisive condition stall in the middle band.

items.prompt: Every wage packet at Oshakati Textiles loses a slice to income tax before it is paid, and every lunch bought at the factory gate carries value-added tax, collected by the seller and added to the bill. Define taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Taxation is the set of compulsory payments a government levies on the incomes, spending or wealth of households and firms, collected to finance public spending; a payment is a tax where the law requires it regardless of any specific service received in return.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: compulsory payments levied on income, spending or wealth to finance public spending, not prices paid for services.

The meaning must carry the direct-versus-indirect boundary the case gives: income tax taken from the wage packet against value-added tax collected by the seller - what the charge falls on, and who hands it over.

items.prompt: The government adds N$6 to the duty on a carton of cigarettes sold at Oshakati's open market, where stalls sell 2 000 cartons a month at N$30 and the state clinic spends N$250 000 a month on the chest cases that follow. Analyse the consequences of the duty for the stallholders, the smokers and the clinic.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the initial change is the duty rising by N$6 a carton, which moves the stall price up from N$30 to N$36, since 30 + 6 = 36. Mechanism: because the price carries more of the harm the clinic pays for, this causes the quantity demanded to tend to fall - some smokers buy fewer cartons, some stop, some switch to cheaper brands or untaxed channels. Consequence: therefore the stallholders sell fewer cartons and their takings may fall even though each carton costs more; the smokers who keep buying pay more of the clinic's cost themselves, and the heaviest smokers are hit hardest in the wallet; and the clinic's case load may ease as buying falls, though where habit keeps demand strong the fall may be small and the duty works mainly as a revenue device. For whom: the stallholder's takings, the smoker's wallet, the clinic's wards and the treasury's receipts each carry their own outcome.
marking_guidance: Starting point: the initial change - the duty rising by N$6, moving the carton from N$30 to N$36 - must be named first.
Mechanism: because the price carries more of the harm the clinic pays for, this causes the quantity demanded to tend to fall.
Consequence: therefore each named party - the stallholders, the smokers, the clinic - needs its own traced outcome.
For whom: name for whom each consequence lands - the stallholder, the smoker, the clinic's patients.

items.prompt: A Katutura clinic spends N$400 000 a season treating the chest cases that follow smoking, and a pack of 20 already carries N$10 of duty at its N$30 price. Explain, for this neighbourhood, why the government taxes tobacco rather than banning it outright.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the figures show the harm - N$400 000 of clinic spending a season - sitting outside the pack's price, with N$10 of duty already moving the price towards carrying part of that harm. The reasoning: because a tax makes the buyer's own price carry more of the cost the clinic bears, it discourages the young and the light smokers first while still raising revenue for the ward, and the link to the choice of tax over ban is that a ban would push the same buying into unrecorded channels where no price signal and no revenue reach the clinic at all. Conclusion: therefore the government taxes rather than bans: the duty raises revenue while steering buying away from tobacco, which a ban would fail to collect and would push underground.
marking_guidance: The context - the figures: N$400 000 of clinic spending against the N$10 already carried by the pack - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the duty moves the price towards carrying the harm, the link is discouragement plus revenue, against a ban's uncollectable underground.
Conclusion: therefore tax rather than ban, with the reason drawn from the data.

items.prompt: Chest wards at the state hospital are full year-round, market traders fear for their trade, and the treasury proposes a further duty rise on tobacco. Discuss whether taxing tobacco more heavily is justified.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement, on balance: a further rise is likely to be justified on health grounds, though it depends on how strongly the quantity demanded responds to the price and on where the revenue lands. Why it might: the duty makes the price carry more of the cost the full wards bear, discouraging new smokers first while steering the rest towards quitting, and the revenue raised can fund the very wards the harm fills - the reasons for taxing a demerit good point the same way. Why it might not: the burden is regressive, falling hardest on poor households whose smokers keep buying; where habit keeps demand strong, the quantity may barely fall and the rise becomes a revenue device rather than a health one; and buying tends to leak into untaxed informal channels, costing the traders their trade while the clinic sees little relief. The condition: what settles it is the responsiveness of the quantity demanded to the price rise - strongly responsive, and the duty is a health measure; weakly responsive, and the rise taxes the poor's habit to fund the harm it causes.
marking_guidance: The judgement must be stated and be decisive: on balance for or against the rise, with its reason.
Why it might: the case for - the price carrying the harm, discouragement and revenue for the wards - developed to its consequence.
Why it might not: the case against - the regressive burden, demand that barely answers the price, leakage into untaxed channels - developed to its own consequence.
The condition it depends on: what settles it is how strongly quantity demanded responds to the price; answers that name no decisive condition stall in the middle band.

items.prompt: At Marula Foods in Gobabis, the company pays tax on its profits out of its own account, while its customers pay value-added tax on every order, added to the bill and handed over by the firm. Define a direct tax and an indirect tax.
items.canonical_answer: A direct tax is a levy whose charge falls on income or profit and is paid over to the revenue authority by the taxed party itself - the company's tax on its profit, paid from its own account. An indirect tax is a levy on spending, collected by a trader from the buyer and passed on - the value-added tax on each order, added to the bill and remitted by Marula Foods.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition of each: the direct tax falls on income or profit and is paid over by the taxed party, while the indirect tax falls on spending and is collected by the seller.
The meaning must hold the boundary the case gives - who hands the charge over, and what it falls on - which is what sorts the two taxes apart.

items.prompt: In one country, a worker earning N$10 000 a month pays N$1 500 of income tax while a worker earning N$30 000 pays N$6 000, and every household, whatever it earns, pays 15 per cent value-added tax on its shopping. Identify the features that make the income tax progressive and the value-added tax regressive in its effect.
items.canonical_answer: The income tax takes a rising share of income: the first worker pays 1 500 / 10 000 = 0.15 of income, or 15 per cent, while the second pays 6 000 / 30 000 = 0.20, or 20 per cent - the share rises with income, which is what makes it progressive. The value-added tax takes the same 15 per cent of spending from every household, but a poorer household spends a larger part of its income, so the tax takes a larger share of that household's income - the feature that makes it regressive in effect.
marking_guidance: Reward the features named - the rising share for the income tax and the larger share of a poor household's income for the value-added tax - as shares, not amounts.

What it includes: a regressive tax is classified by the share of income it takes, not by a falling rate; a value-added tax at a flat rate is regressive because the poor spend a larger part of their incomes.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A duty rise at Walvis Bay lifted the price of a litre of fuel, and haulage firms have since cut their routes; one firm's ledger also shows income tax paid on its profits, straight from its own account. Explain, for this port town, the classification of the two taxes and the direction in which the events ran.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the extract shows two charges on one haulier - a duty collected from buyers at the pump and passed on by fuel stations, and a profit tax paid over by the firm itself. The reasoning: the duty is an indirect tax, levied on spending and collected by the seller; the profit tax is a direct tax, levied on income and handed over by the taxed firm, and the link to the route cuts is direction: the duty rise pushed fuel costs up, and the route cuts followed - the cuts are consequences of the increase in taxes, not the cause of it. Conclusion: therefore the classification is settled by who pays the charge over and what it falls on, and the story runs from the tax change to the routes, not the other way round.
marking_guidance: The context - the data: the duty at the pump against the profit tax paid from the firm's own account - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the sorting turns on what the charge falls on and who hands it over, the link is the direct-against-indirect boundary.
Conclusion: therefore the direction must be stated plainly - the duty rise is the cause, the route cuts are consequences of an increase in taxes, never the cause of it.

items.prompt: Namibia's income tax is deducted from wages before they are paid, its rates are published in advance, and its rules state plainly what is due from whom and when. Define the principles of taxation this system shows.
items.canonical_answer: The principles of taxation are the standards a tax system is judged against: equity, that those more able to pay bear a larger share; certainty, that the payer knows what is due, when and how; convenience, that payment is easy where and when it falls due; and economy, that the tax costs little to collect relative to what it raises. Deduction before payment shows convenience; rates published in advance show certainty.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: the four principles - equity, certainty, convenience and economy - each stated as its standard.
The meaning must attach the principles to the system's features named in the prompt; a bare list with no standard attached earns little.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: In one country the income tax rates for the year ahead are published before the year begins; in another they are announced after incomes have been earned and spent. Explain why certainty is treated as a principle of good taxation.
items.canonical_answer: Certainty is a principle because a payer who knows in advance what is due, when and how can plan spending, saving and work around the charge, so the tax bears on choices without unsettling them and the revenue flows steadily; where rates change without notice, payers cannot know what an hour of work or a season of trading will leave them, so effort and investment tend to shrink, disputes with the authority rise, and the revenue the tax raises turns unreliable. The purpose of the principle is to hold the system to a standard the payer can see, and the reason it ranks with equity is that an unpredictable tax, however fair on paper, fails the payer in practice.
marking_guidance: The reason or purpose of the principle must be stated: a payer who knows what is due can plan, so the revenue flows steadily.
Why it matters must run through the contrast the prompt gives - rates known in advance against rates announced after the fact - each with its consequence.
Because the reason runs through choices, reward the link between certainty and the effort and investment households and firms make.
items.provenance: Authored under standard v0.2.0-draft from the topic claim ledger.

items.prompt: A market trader at Katima Mulilo pays a flat N$20 daily stall fee whatever her takings, while her cousin, a salaried engineer in Windhoek, has income tax deducted from a wage that rises with each promotion. Explain, from these two cases, which system better follows the equity principle and why.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the figures show a flat N$20 a day from the trader whatever her earnings, against tax deducted from a wage that rises with promotion. The reasoning: equity asks that those with a greater ability to pay bear a larger share, and the link is that the fee takes the same N$20 from a thin day's takings and from a good one - a larger share of a poor trader's income - while the engineer's tax rises with each pay rise, so the wage-based system follows equity more closely; the fee does score on economy, being cheap to collect. Conclusion: therefore judged on the equity principle the salary-based system is the fairer, though the trading fee buys simplicity, and the choice between them trades one principle against another.
marking_guidance: The context - the data: the flat N$20 fee against the rising deduction from the engineer's wage - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because equity turns on ability to pay, the link is the share each system takes from thin earnings against rising ones.
Conclusion: therefore the salary-based system better follows equity, with the fee's economy acknowledged as the trade-off.

items.prompt: A nurse at Otjiwarongo takes home less than her gross wage once income tax has been deducted. Define disposable income, the channel through which income tax affects households.
items.canonical_answer: Disposable income is the income households have left to spend or save after tax and other compulsory deductions have been taken from their gross income; an income tax lowers it directly, which is why its impact on households runs through their spending.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: income left after deductions, with income tax's impact running through it.
The meaning must show the channel: a tax that lowers disposable income lowers what households can spend and save.

items.prompt: Income tax rates rise across Oshakati, and 8 000 nurses, teachers and lodge workers each keep less of their pay each month. Analyse the consequences for these households, the shops they buy from and the treasury.
items.canonical_answer: Starting point: the initial change is a higher income tax rate, lowering each worker's disposable income - the slice of the wage left after deductions. Mechanism: because household spending tends to follow disposable income, this causes less to be spent in the shops, on transport and on services, and where the rise is steep some workers may put in less overtime or move income into untaxed work. Consequence: therefore the households buy less and save less; the shops and services see fewer sales and may trim staff hours, spreading the effect to other workers; and the treasury may find the rise yields less than forecast if spending weakens and taxpaying work shrinks. For whom: the worker's take-home pay, the shopkeeper's takings, the treasury's receipts - each needs its own traced outcome.

Consequence: therefore each named party - the households, the shops, the treasury - needs its own traced outcome.

items.prompt: Fuel duty of N$3 a litre is added at Swakopmund's pumps, and a tour operator there fills a 50-litre tank each working day, 22 days a month. Explain, using these figures, the impact of the duty on the operator and the passengers.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the figures show the duty adding N$150 to each tank, since 3 x 50 = 150, and about N$3 300 across the month, since 150 x 22 = 3 300 - a sum the operator must find from fares or margins. The reasoning: because fuel is a cost of every tour, this causes fares to rise or trips to be trimmed, and the link to the passengers is a dearer ticket for the same journey, with some travellers choosing fewer trips; where competition holds fares down, the operator's margin bears more of the duty instead. Conclusion: therefore the duty steers the operator towards fuller vehicles and the passengers towards fewer journeys, while the treasury collects the N$3 300 - and where passengers are few and the vehicles must run anyway, the margin absorbs it.
marking_guidance: The context - the figures: N$150 a tank and about N$3 300 a month - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because the duty is a cost of every journey, the link runs to fares, to trips trimmed and to the operator's margin.
Conclusion: therefore the impact lands on the operator's costs, the passengers' fares and the quantity of journeys.

items.prompt: With work scarce in the northern regions, one budget raises public works spending and cuts the duty on building materials; with prices climbing in the south, another budget freezes the public wage bill and raises a duty. Define the fiscal policy measures these budgets show.
items.canonical_answer: An expansionary measure raises government spending or cuts taxes to lift total spending in the economy, fitting the northern budget's raised public works and cut duty; a contractionary measure cuts spending or raises taxes to slow it, fitting the southern budget's freeze and rise. The measures are defined by their direction: expansionary where total spending in the economy is judged too weak, contractionary where prices are judged to be climbing too fast.
marking_guidance: Reward the precise definition: expansionary measures raise spending or cut taxes to lift total spending in the economy; contractionary ones cut or raise to slow it.

items.prompt: With workshops idle across Otavi and unemployment high, the budget raises public spending on the town's water scheme by N$40 million a year and borrows the sum rather than raising taxes. Analyse how these measures work through Otavi's economy and its future budgets.

items.prompt: Prices in Windhoek have climbed for six months running, and the budget answers by freezing the public wage bill and raising the duty on new vehicles. Explain, from these measures, how a contractionary fiscal stance is meant to slow the climb.

Conclusion: therefore the stance leans against the climb by trimming what households and firms can spend, though the freeze also bears on the public workers' own living costs, and where rising costs - fuel, imported goods - push the climb, the measures may slow it rather than stop it.

items.prompt: Oshakati's public health spending has grown for five years, the town's debt repayments have grown with it, and 6 000 young people sit on the unemployment register. Explain, from these facts, how fiscal policy's effects can move two macroeconomic aims against one another.
items.canonical_answer: The context: the data show a budget that has expanded health spending year on year, financed by borrowing whose repayments now weigh on the same budget, in a town where 6 000 young people are out of work. The reasoning: because the health spending serves the health of the town - and where there is spare capacity, sustained public spending also supports jobs - the link runs through the borrowing: the repayment line crowds out spending that might otherwise hire or train the registered young, so the government faces a choice between the health gains and the employment aim. Conclusion: therefore the two aims - health now against jobs for the young - move against one another through the budget constraint the borrowing creates; a fiscal choice to spend on one is, through the repayment line, a choice against the other.
marking_guidance: The context - the data: five years of growing health spending and repayments against 6 000 registered young - must anchor the answer.
Reasoning: because borrowing links the two, the link is the repayment line crowding out the employment-serving spending.
Conclusion: therefore the two aims move against one another through the budget constraint, with the trade stated plainly.

items.prompt:
Eight questions in the style of Paper 1. Choose one option for each.

1. The government budget is best defined as:
A  the record of last year's tax receipts
B  the yearly plan of expected revenue and intended spending
C  the stock of money the government holds
D  the law that sets up the revenue authority

2. A country's imports of goods and services exceed its exports, while its government's revenue exceeds its spending. The country has:
A  a budget deficit and a current account surplus
B  a budget surplus and a current account deficit
C  both a budget deficit and a current account deficit
D  a balanced budget and a current account surplus

3. A tax is:
A  a payment for a service received from the state
B  a compulsory levy on income, spending or wealth
C  a penalty imposed on law-breakers
D  a loan the government repays with interest

4. Which is an indirect tax?
A  income tax on a nurse's wage
B  company tax on a firm's profit
C  value-added tax added to a shop bill
D  a weekly levy on each worker's wage

5. An income tax is progressive where:
A  everyone pays the same amount
B  the share of income taken rises as income rises
C  the share of income taken falls as income rises
D  the rate is the same whatever the payer earns

6. After a fuel duty rise, a haulier cut two routes. Which states the direction correctly?
A  the duty rise caused the route cuts
B  the route cuts caused the duty rise
C  the two events are unrelated
D  the duty rise and the cuts are the same event

7. Which is a fiscal policy measure?
A  raising the interest rate banks charge
B  raising the standard rate of income tax
C  lowering the price of foreign currency
D  licensing a second mobile operator

8. Fiscal policy is the use of:
A  interest rates and lending rules
B  government spending, taxation and borrowing
C  laws to control dominant sellers
D  duties charged on imported goods alone
items.canonical_answer:
1 B. The budget is a plan for the year ahead pairing revenue with spending. A catches the learner who treats the budget as a record of the past rather than a plan; C catches the confusion of the budget with the government's cash; D catches the confusion of the budget with the law that creates the tax office.
2 B. Revenue above spending is a budget surplus; imports above exports is a current account deficit. A and C catch the budget-deficit-versus-current-account-deficit confusion, treating the two balances as one; D catches the learner who reads one surplus as both.
3 B. A tax is compulsory and owed regardless of service. A catches the learner who treats a tax as a price; C catches the confusion of taxes with penalties; D catches the confusion of taxes with borrowing.
4 C. Value-added tax is levied on spending and collected by the seller. A and B catch the learner who classifies the income and profit charges as indirect; D catches the boundary drawn the wrong way round - a levy on a wage, handed over from it, is direct.
5 B. Progression turns on the share of income rising with income. A catches the confusion of progressive with a flat amount; C states the regressive case; D catches the confusion of progressive with proportional in rate terms.
6 A. The tax change is the cause and the route cuts are its consequence. B catches the confusion the register records - consequences of an increase in taxes written as its cause; C and D catch accounts that abandon the direction of events altogether.
7 B. A tax change is the budget's own lever. A catches the learner who reaches for the interest rate - the price of borrowing - which is monetary policy's lever, not fiscal policy's; C catches the exchange-rate confusion; D catches the confusion of fiscal policy with regulation.
8 B. The three levers are spending, taxation and borrowing. A catches the interest-rate confusion again; C catches the confusion with competition policy; D narrows fiscal policy to one narrow duty and catches the learner who forgets the spending and borrowing levers.
marking_guidance: One mark per question; the key and the distractor explanations are the teaching back of the set.

Each distractor explanation names the specific misunderstanding it catches - the direct-versus-indirect boundary, the consequence-versus-cause direction, the interest-rate-versus-tax confusion, and the budget-versus-current-account balances.
Questions 2, 4 and 6 carry the topic's registered misconceptions, so their distractor explanations are the discrimination itself.

facts: P01 covers the budget definition and deficit balances, the nature and classification of taxes, and the definition of fiscal policy

items.prompt:
A radio report from Oshakati, May 2027: "The town council is weighing a N$2 a litre levy on sugary drinks sold through the town's 40 licensed outlets. The state clinic's wards treated 3 000 sugar-related cases last year, and the council met N$4.5 million of their cost. Outlets sold 300 000 litres last year at prices the levy would raise."

Table 1 - the levy, as proposed
  rate: N$2 a litre
  litres sold last year: 300 000
  clinic cost met by the council: N$4.5 million
  outlets covered: 40

(a) Calculate the revenue the levy would have raised on last year's sales. [1]
(b) Identify from the report one feature that makes the levy an indirect tax, and one reason the council is weighing it. [2]
(c) Explain why the levy's burden may weigh more heavily on poorer households in Oshakati. [4]
(d) Analyse what the levy would do to the town's drinking, its outlets and the clinic, using the data as evidence. [6]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) 300 000 x 2 = 600 000; the levy would have raised N$600 000 on last year's litres.
(b) The levy is added to the price of each litre and collected by the outlet from the buyer - a tax on spending collected by traders, which is what makes it indirect. The council is weighing it to make the price carry more of the N$4.5 million of clinic cost that drinking imposes on others, and to discourage the drinking that fills the wards.
(c) A poorer household spends a larger part of its income on drinks and food generally, so the same N$2 a litre takes a larger share of a poor household's income than of a rich one's - the levy is regressive in effect. Because poorer households also tend to buy the sugary drinks most heavily, they bear more of the charge; and where they keep buying out of habit, they are less able than richer households to switch to untaxed choices.
(d) The expected relationship: the levy raises the price, and the quantity of sugary drinks demanded tends to fall, easing the harm the wards pay for. The evidence: 300 000 litres sold against a N$4.5 million clinic bill, with the N$2 rate raising N$600 000 towards that bill if litres held. The analysis: for the outlets, fewer litres spread across 40 counters trims takings and may cut staff hours; for the drinkers, the price rise steers the light buyers first, while the heaviest keep buying and bear the regressive weight; for the clinic, a slower flow of sugar-related cases eases the N$4.5 million burden, and the levy's revenue can fund the wards directly. The exception: where habit keeps demand strong, litres may fall very little, the wards see little relief, and the levy works mainly as a revenue device raised on the poor's spending.
marking_guidance: Parts (a) and (b) are read from the data; the six-mark part must use the figures as evidence - the 300 000 litres, the N$2 rate, the N$4.5 million - not as analysis itself.
One mark per distinct linked statement in (c) and (d): a relationship, a reason or a named consequence counts where it is linked, not merely listed.
Part (d) is marked on expected relationship, then evidence, then analysis, then an exception; quoting figures without the relationship they support earns nothing.
For whom: consequences must be named for the outlets, the drinkers and the clinic, each with its own traced outcome.

facts: clinic cost met by the council N$4.5 million

items.prompt:
Answer all parts.

(a) Define fiscal policy. [2]
(b) Explain two reasons why the government, rather than private firms, funds the Otavi water scheme and the clinics that serve it. [4]
(c) The budget raises public spending on a new district training college by N$40 million a year, funded by borrowing, with 300 builders idle in the district and construction firms working below capacity. Analyse the effects of this measure on the macroeconomic aims of employment, growth and price stability. [6]
(d) Discuss whether the government should cut income taxes rather than raise spending when unemployment is high but prices are climbing. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Fiscal policy is the use of government spending, taxation and borrowing to influence the economy, with the yearly budget as its instrument.
(b) The water scheme is close to a public good: clean water for the town's households cannot sensibly be confined to those who pay, so a private firm would tend to provide too little of it - the government funds it because the market left alone would under-provide. The clinics are merit goods: households undervalue check-ups and treatment until illness makes them urgent, so left to pay directly they would consume less than the district's health requires; public funding corrects that under-consumption. The two reasons - the under-provided public good and the under-consumed merit good - are the standard cases for public spending.
(c) Starting point: the initial change is N$40 million a year of public spending on the college, financed by borrowing, arriving in a district with 300 builders idle and firms working below capacity - clear spare capacity. Mechanism: because the building work hires the idle builders and sends orders to construction firms, this causes incomes to rise and circulate through the district's suppliers and shops; with capacity spare, the extra spending tends to raise output and employment rather than prices. Consequence: therefore the growth aim gains as output rises, the employment aim gains as the builders and further workers are drawn in, and the price-stability aim holds while capacity is spare - though as capacity tightens, later spending tends to push prices up, and the borrowing weighs on future budgets, whose repayments fall on later taxpayers. For whom: the builders and firms now, the district's shops through the wage chain, the later taxpayer at the repayment line.
(d) A tax cut answers high unemployment quickly: it lifts disposable income at once, and where there is spare capacity the extra spending tends to raise output and jobs rather than prices, with the payroll already in place to deliver it. Why it might not: with prices climbing already, the same extra spending tends to add pressure to prices as capacity tightens, so the cut risks moving one aim against another; a cut in the standard rate gives more to higher earners, so its reach is regressive; and the revenue it surrenders widens the budget gap, shifting repayment onto later budgets. The judgement, on balance: where unemployment is the sharper problem and capacity is plainly spare, the cut is justified; the condition it depends on is how close the economy is to full capacity - the closer, the more the case turns to targeted spending or to holding the stance.
marking_guidance: Every part carries a model answer; part (d) is level-marked over three bands.
(a) rewards the precise definition: spending, taxation and borrowing used to influence the economy.
(b) one mark per distinct reason with its link made: the public-good case and the merit-good case, each carried to its consequence.

(c) one mark per distinct linked statement from the starting point - N$40 million arriving where 300 builders are idle - through the mechanism to the consequence for each named aim; the spare-capacity condition earns its place.

(d) Level 3 examines why it might - spending power and jobs where capacity is spare - and why it might not - pressure on prices, regressive reach, the wider gap - and reaches a judgement naming the condition it depends on; Level 2 develops one side; Level 1 asserts.

facts: training college spending N$40 million a year, funded by borrowing

items.prompt: Plan an answer to: "The budget deficit stands at N$8 billion in a year when workshops sit idle. Discuss whether the government should borrow less." Do not write the essay; produce the plan.
items.canonical_answer:
Case for borrowing less: the deficit shifts today's spending onto future taxpayers, who meet the interest from later budgets. Chain 1: borrowing falls -> programmes are trimmed or taxes rise -> spending across the economy falls -> where workshops already sit idle, output and jobs fall further (for the taxpayer, and for the worker).
Case against borrowing less - for holding or raising it: with capacity spare, public spending tends to raise output and employment rather than prices. Chain 2: borrowed funds build the water scheme or the college -> the idle workshops are hired -> household incomes rise and the tax base widens -> later repayments are met from a larger output (for the worker, the firm, the later taxpayer).
Judgement: the case for borrowing turns on the condition - where the funds buy capacity-raising projects and the economy has spare capacity, the N$8 billion is justified; where they fund current consumption near full capacity, borrowing less is the better course.
marking_guidance: A plan, not an essay: the structure with the stated judgement is what is assessed.
The plan must carry the case for and the case against, each developed as a chain from the measure to its consequence, and name the parties - the worker, the taxpayer, the later taxpayer.
The judgement must be decisive and name the condition it depends on: what the borrowed funds buy, and how much capacity is spare.
What settles it: whether the borrowing raises the economy's productive capacity against merely funding the present - the decisive test is what the funds buy and the state of capacity.

facts: workshops idle - spare capacity in the economy
